title: Moles, Equations and Energy in Reactions
seo_title: Year 11 Chemistry: Moles and Chemical Reactions Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_code: Chemistry Unit 1: Chemical reactions: reactants, products and energy
standard_text: The mole concept and molar mass; empirical and molecular formulae; balanced equations and mass calculations; limiting reactants; exothermic and endothermic reactions, energy profiles, enthalpy change and calorimetry. (Senior Secondary Chemistry, Unit 1: Chemical fundamentals: structure, properties and reactions)
meta_desc: Free Year 11 Chemistry worksheets on the mole, molar mass, empirical formulae, balancing equations, mass calculations, limiting reactants, ΔH and calorimetry. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: q = mcΔT; ΔH = −q ÷ n for an exothermic reaction.
body_html:
How to think about it

The mole counts particles: 1 mol = 6.02 × 10²³ particles, and n = m ÷ M. A balanced equation gives mole ratios, so you can find the mass of product from the mass of reactant: mass → moles → ratio → moles → mass.

Reactions are exothermic (ΔH negative) or endothermic (ΔH positive). In calorimetry the heat absorbed by water is q = m × 4.18 × ΔT; divide by the moles of fuel to find the molar enthalpy.

Example

Moles in 11.0 g of CO₂ (M = 44.0 g/mol)?

n = 11.0 ÷ 44.0

Answer: 0.250 mol

Example

0.010 mol of fuel heats 200 g of water by 10 K. ΔH?

q = 200 × 4.18 × 10 = 8360 J

8.36 kJ ÷ 0.010 mol

Answer: −836 kJ/mol

Common mistakes

  • Using the mass ratio instead of the mole ratio from the equation.
  • Forgetting the negative sign of ΔH for an exothermic reaction.
  • Changing a formula (subscript) to balance an equation.

faq.q: How do you find the limiting reactant?
faq.a: Work out the moles of each reactant and divide by its coefficient; the smallest value is the limiting reactant, which decides the amount of product.

faq.q: What is the difference between ΔH and activation energy?
faq.a: ΔH is the energy difference between reactants and products; the activation energy is the energy barrier the reactants must get over.

What percent of the mass of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is O? (H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23; molar mass = 40 g/mol)

What is an endothermic reaction?

one that happens only in sunlight
one that absorbs energy from the surroundings, so ΔH is positive
items.e: Photosynthesis and thermal decomposition are endothermic.

items.q: What is an exothermic reaction?
c: one that takes in energy, so ΔH is positive
one that releases energy to the surroundings, so ΔH is negative
items.e: Combustion and neutralisation are exothermic.

items.q: What is the empirical formula of a compound?
c: the actual number of atoms in a molecule
the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element
items.e: Glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ has the empirical formula CH₂O.

items.q: What percent of the mass of magnesium oxide (MgO) is O? (O = 16, Mg = 24; molar mass = 40 g/mol)
Calculate the relative formula mass of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH.

items.q: Is this equation balanced? 2Na + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → 4NaOH + H<sub>2</sub>
c: Yes. Both sides have the same elements.
No. H has 4 atoms on the left and 6 on the right.
No. There are too many arrows.
items.e: Count each element on both sides.

items.q: What number replaces ? to balance the equation? ?SO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2SO<sub>3</sub>
items.e: Balanced: 2SO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2SO<sub>3</sub>.

items.q: Is this equation balanced? Al<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> + 6NaOH → 2Al(OH)<sub>3</sub> + 3Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
c: Yes. Each element has the same number of atoms on both sides.
No. There are more molecules on the right.
items.e: Count each element on both sides.

c: No. H has 8 atoms on the left and 2 on the right.
No. There are too many arrows.

items.e: Balanced: N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 2NH<sub>3</sub>.

items.q: A compound contains C 75.0%, H 25.0% by mass. What is its empirical formula?
items.e: Divide each % by A<sub>r</sub>, then divide by the smallest: C 6.25, H 25.0.

items.q: A compound contains Fe 69.9%, O 30.1% by mass. What is its empirical formula?
items.e: Divide each % by A<sub>r</sub>, then divide by the smallest: Fe 1.25, O 1.88.

items.q: What number replaces ? to balance the equation? ?Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO
items.e: Balanced: 2Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO.

items.q: A compound contains Al 52.9%, O 47.1% by mass. What is its empirical formula?
items.e: Divide each % by A<sub>r</sub>, then divide by the smallest: Al 1.96, O 2.94.

items.q: A compound contains C 54.5%, H 9.10%, O 36.4% by mass. What is its empirical formula?
items.e: Divide each % by A<sub>r</sub>, then divide by the smallest: C 4.54, H 9.10, O 2.27.

items.q: A compound contains Na 32.4%, S 22.6%, O 45.0% by mass. What is its empirical formula?
items.e: Divide each % by A<sub>r</sub>, then divide by the smallest: Na 1.41, S 0.704, O 2.81.

items.e: Balanced: Cu + 2AgNO<sub>3</sub> → Cu(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + 2Ag.

c: No. There are more molecules on the right.
Yes. Each element has the same number of atoms on both sides.
items.e: Count each element on both sides.

items.q: What number replaces ? to balance the equation? Zn + ?HCl → ZnCl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>
items.e: Balanced: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>.

items.q: When magnesium burns: 2Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO. What mass of MgO form from 96 g of O<sub>2</sub>? (O<sub>2</sub> = 32 g/mol, MgO = 40 g/mol)
When sodium reacts with chlorine: 2Na + Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2NaCl. You start with 8 mol of Na and 5 mol of Cl<sub>2</sub>. How many moles of NaCl can form?
items.e: Na is limiting; it gives 8 mol of NaCl.

items.q: For CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, 1.50 mol of CH₄ reacts with 3.50 mol of O₂. Which is the limiting reagent?
items.e: Divide moles by the coefficients: 1.50 ÷ 1 = 1.50 and 3.50 ÷ 2 = 1.75. The smaller one, CH₄, runs out first.

items.q: When an acid is neutralized: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2NaOH → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O. You start with 2 mol of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and 10 mol of NaOH. Which is the limiting reactant?
items.e: The equation needs H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> : NaOH = 1 : 2; 2 mol H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> ÷ 1 = 2, 10 mol NaOH ÷ 2 = 5. The smaller one runs out first.

items.q: When aluminium reacts with acid: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl<sub>3</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>. What mass of H<sub>2</sub> form from 73 g of HCl? (HCl = 36.5 g/mol, H<sub>2</sub> = 2 g/mol)

When propane burns in a grill: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O. You start with 3 mol of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> and 2 mol of O<sub>2</sub>. How many moles of CO<sub>2</sub> can form?
items.e: O<sub>2</sub> is limiting; it gives 1.2 mol of CO<sub>2</sub>.

items.q: When iron is made in a blast gas heater: Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO<sub>2</sub>. What mass of Fe form along with 132 g of CO<sub>2</sub>? (CO<sub>2</sub> = 44 g/mol, Fe = 56 g/mol)
When magnesium burns: 2Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO. What mass of MgO form from 128 g of O<sub>2</sub>? (O<sub>2</sub> = 32 g/mol, MgO = 40 g/mol)
When aluminium reacts with acid: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl<sub>3</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>. What mass of Al react with 36.5 g of HCl? (HCl = 36.5 g/mol, Al = 27 g/mol)
5.00 g of N<sub>2</sub> reacts completely: N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 2NH<sub>3</sub>. Calculate the maximum (theoretical) mass of NH<sub>3</sub>.
For C + O₂ → CO₂, 2.00 mol of C reacts with 2.50 mol of O₂. Which is the limiting reagent?
items.e: Divide moles by the coefficients: 2.00 ÷ 1 = 2.00 and 2.50 ÷ 1 = 2.50. The smaller one, C, runs out first.

items.q: When ammonia is made from nitrogen and hydrogen: N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 2NH<sub>3</sub>. You start with 10 mol of N<sub>2</sub> and 4 mol of H<sub>2</sub>. Which is the limiting reactant?
items.e: The equation needs N<sub>2</sub> : H<sub>2</sub> = 1 : 3; 10 mol N<sub>2</sub> ÷ 1 = 10, 4 mol H<sub>2</sub> ÷ 3 = 1.33. The smaller one runs out first.

items.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, 4.50 mol of N₂ reacts with 2.50 mol of H₂. Which is the limiting reagent?
items.e: Divide moles by the coefficients: 4.50 ÷ 1 = 4.50 and 2.50 ÷ 3 = 0.833. The smaller one, H₂, runs out first.

items.q: For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 3.50 mol of H₂ reacts with 6.00 mol of O₂. What mass of H₂O forms? (molar mass of H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹)
items.e: The limiting reagent decides the amount: 1.75 × 2 mol × 18 g mol⁻¹ = 63.0 g.

items.q: When ethane burns: 2C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + 7O<sub>2</sub> → 4CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O. You start with 8 mol of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> and 3 mol of O<sub>2</sub>. Which is the limiting reactant?
items.e: The equation needs C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> : O<sub>2</sub> = 2 : 7; 8 mol C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> ÷ 2 = 4, 3 mol O<sub>2</sub> ÷ 7 = 0.43. The smaller one runs out first.

items.q: For C + O₂ → CO₂, 4.00 mol of C reacts with 3.50 mol of O₂. Which is the limiting reagent?
items.e: Divide moles by the coefficients: 4.00 ÷ 1 = 4.00 and 3.50 ÷ 1 = 3.50. The smaller one, O₂, runs out first.

items.q: When aluminium reacts with acid: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl<sub>3</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>. You start with 6 mol of Al and 12 mol of HCl. Which is the limiting reactant?
items.e: The equation needs Al : HCl = 2 : 6; 6 mol Al ÷ 2 = 3, 12 mol HCl ÷ 6 = 2. The smaller one runs out first.

items.q: When sodium reacts with chlorine: 2Na + Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2NaCl. You start with 10 mol of Na and 12 mol of Cl<sub>2</sub>. How many moles of NaCl can form?
items.e: Na is limiting; it gives 10 mol of NaCl.

items.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, 4.50 mol of N₂ reacts with 3.50 mol of H₂. What mass of NH₃ forms? (molar mass of NH₃ = 17 g mol⁻¹)
items.e: The limiting reagent decides the amount: 1.17 × 2 mol × 17 g mol⁻¹ = 39.7 g.

items.q: When aluminium reacts with oxygen: 4Al + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>. You start with 6 mol of Al and 10 mol of O<sub>2</sub>. Which is the limiting reactant?
items.e: The equation needs Al : O<sub>2</sub> = 4 : 3; 6 mol Al ÷ 4 = 1.5, 10 mol O<sub>2</sub> ÷ 3 = 3.33. The smaller one runs out first.

items.q: Which equation links amount, mass and molar mass?
items.e: Amount (mol) = mass (g) ÷ molar mass (g/mol).

items.q: What is the products of the complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
items.e: Incomplete combustion can give CO and soot.

items.q: Why must a chemical equation be balanced?
c: atoms are neither created nor destroyed, so each element must have the same number on both sides
to show the reaction is fast
so the molecules have the same mass
so the charges are all zero
items.e: Change only the coefficients, never the formulae.

items.q: 2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O. Bond energies (kJ/mol): H–H = 436, O=O = 498, O–H = 463. How much energy is released when the product bonds form?
2H<sub>2</sub>O → 2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub>. Bond energies (kJ/mol): O–H = 463, H–H = 436, O=O = 498. How much energy is released when the product bonds form?
H<sub>2</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2HCl. Bond energies (kJ/mol): H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 242, H–Cl = 431. How much energy is needed to break the bonds in the reactants?

items.q: Why does a calorimetry experiment usually give a smaller value of ΔH than the data book?
c: heat is lost to the surroundings and the combustion may be incomplete
items.e: Insulating the calorimeter reduces the loss.

items.q: What is the mole?
c: the amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles
the volume of 1 L of gas
items.e: This number is Avogadro's constant.

items.q: 2H<sub>2</sub>O → 2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub>. Bond energies (kJ/mol): O–H = 463, H–H = 436, O=O = 498. What is the energy change?
items.e: the energy change = broken − formed = 1852 − 1370 = +482 kJ.

items.e: Reverse Ea = peak − products = 90 − 30 = 60 kJ.

items.q: In an energy profile diagram, what is the activation energy?
c: the energy difference between reactants and products
the energy released by the reaction
the energy difference between the reactants and the top of the energy barrier
items.e: ΔH is reactants to products; Ea is reactants to the peak.

items.e: the energy change = broken − formed = 1370 − 1852 = −482 kJ.

items.q: 2HI → H<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>2</sub>. Bond energies (kJ/mol): H–I = 299, H–H = 436, I–I = 151. What is the energy change?
items.e: the energy change = broken − formed = 598 − 587 = +11 kJ.

items.q: H<sub>2</sub> + F<sub>2</sub> → 2HF. Bond energies (kJ/mol): H–H = 436, F–F = 158, H–F = 567. What is the energy change?
items.e: the energy change = broken − formed = 594 − 1134 = −540 kJ.

items.q: H<sub>2</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2HCl. Bond energies (kJ/mol): H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 242, H–Cl = 431. What is the energy change?
items.e: the energy change = broken − formed = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ.

items.q: Why is incomplete combustion of fuels dangerous?
c: it can make carbon monoxide, a toxic gas
items.e: CO binds to haemoglobin.

items.q: Burning 0.30 g of propan-1-ol (M<sub>r</sub> 60.0) heats 100 g of water by 30.0 K. Calculate the enthalpy of combustion (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹).
items.e: q = mcΔT = 12500 J; n = 0.00500 mol; the energy change = −q/n = −2510 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: 25.0 mL of 1.0 mol/L HCl is mixed with 25.0 mL of 1.0 mol/L NaOH. The temperature rises by 6.4 K. Calculate the enthalpy of neutralisation (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹).
items.e: q = mcΔT = 50.0 × 4.18 × 6.4 = 1340 J; n = 0.0250 mol; the energy change = −q/n = −53.5 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Burning 0.25 g of hexane (M<sub>r</sub> 86.0) heats 200 g of water by 25.0 K. Calculate the enthalpy of combustion (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹).
